newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions pact with gov't on labor reforms.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions pact with gov't on labor reforms.

text.p: Argentina's largest labor federation, the CGT, said Friday it had reached a preliminary agreement on labor reform with the Peronist government that could mean it dropping plans for a general strike this month.
The deal, thrashed out in a marathon secret session beginning Wednesday night and ending Thursday, must first be submitted to businessmen for approval to become effective.

"There is a preliminary deal," one CGT official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters. "Some businessmen have already expressed their approval, but it needs the formal approval of all the Group of Eight (major business lobbies)."

Three-way negotiations between President Carlos Menem's government, the unions and business leaders in March had broken down over Menem's plans to reform labor legislation as requested by the International Monetary Fund and the business community.
Menem argues that reforms would help combat current unemployment of over 17 percent.

The reforms proposed by the president include swapping redundancy payouts for unemployment insurance and, allowing workers to make salary and labor condition deals directly with employers with no centralized union intervention.
He is also pushing for the complete deregulation of the union-controlled private health system.

Unions, fearing workers would lose rights and they would lose influence and income, have fought back with strikes and are backed by the courts, who objected to Menem's attempts to reform by decree rather than through Congress.

The CGT official said the threat of a 24-hour general strike this month "still stands and has not been modified at all." CGT leaer Rodolfo Daer has also warned of a further 36-hour strike in June if there is no progress on labor talks, but is under pressure from union hardliners to first name a date for May's stoppage.

However the union official said that if a three-way pact on labor reforms were signed soon between the government, the unions and business leaders, "we would be getting the solutions we need, so there would be no reason for a strike."
One of the first business leaders to react to the announcement of a preliminary deal was the head of the Argentine Chamber of Commerce, Jorge Di Fiori.
Given a copy of the deal by Menem's negotiators, Di Fiori played down the idea that the agreement was struck behind the back of business leaders, telling reporters:
"There is for example some progress on the issue of redundancy pay and the creation of a fund to substitute that, which was one of the things that met resistance."

He said the deal also allowed for open competition in healthcare -- but only among union healthcare systems, whereas government and businesses want the union healthcare funds to compete with private healthcare companies.

"This is a preliminary agreement and it was explained to us that it has not been signed because that would make it only a two-way agreement, whereas the government wants a three-way deal with business leaders involved," said Di Fiori.
